result.summary: Hercules performs his eleventh labour, fetching the golden apples of the Hesperides, overcoming many hosts and monsters on the way and tricking Atlas. He then performs his twelfth labour, descending to Hades and bringing back Cerberus.

scenes.title: Apples assigned; Cycnus challenges
scenes.summary: Eurystheus orders the apples; the dragon and Hesperides are described. Hercules meets Cycnus, and a thunderbolt parts the fighters.
scenes.stakes: Hercules risks death in single combat against a son of Ares.

scenes.title: Seizing Nereus
scenes.summary: Hercules goes to the nymphs by the Eridanus and binds the shape-shifting Nereus until he reveals the way.
scenes.stakes: Hercules needs the knowledge to find the apples.

scenes.title: Wrestling Antaeus in Libya
scenes.summary: Hercules kills Antaeus by lifting him from the earth.
scenes.stakes: Death by wrestling, as befell Antaeus's victims.

scenes.title: Busiris and the altar
scenes.summary: Seized to be sacrificed in Egypt, Hercules bursts his bonds and kills Busiris and Amphidamas.
scenes.stakes: Hercules is about to be sacrificed on the altar.

scenes.title: Lindos, Arabia and Caucasus
scenes.summary: Hercules sacrifices a bullock, kills Emathion, receives the goblet from the Sun, and frees Prometheus, shooting the eagle.

scenes.title: Tricking Atlas
scenes.summary: Hercules relieves Atlas, who tries to leave him the sky; Hercules tricks him back under it and takes the apples to Eurystheus.
scenes.stakes: Hercules could be stuck holding up the sky forever.

scenes.title: Initiation at Eleusis
scenes.summary: Before fetching Cerberus, Hercules is cleansed and initiated by Eumolpus.
scenes.stakes: Without cleansing he cannot see the mysteries.

scenes.title: Descent to Hades
scenes.summary: Hercules descends at Taenarum, frees Theseus, wrestles Menoetes, subdues Cerberus, and returns him after showing Eurystheus.
scenes.stakes: Hercules must master Cerberus without weapons, facing the dead.

notable_quotes.reason: Hercules's trick that sends the sky back onto Atlas.

analysis.text: Hercules wins by strength and cunning, mastering death itself in the descent to Hades.
The passage preserves variant traditions and ritual origins, such as the cursing sacrifice at Lindos and initiation at Eleusis.

legacy.text: Atlas holding the sky and Hercules's trick became a classic subject in Greek and Roman art, including the Olympia metope.
Cerberus appears as the guard of the underworld in many works, including the Harry Potter novels as Fluffy (1997).

fun_facts.text: The Library is attributed to Apollodorus, but is now thought to date from the first or second century AD.

language_notes.text: Eurystheus refused to count two labours: the Hydra, because Iolaus helped, and the Augean stables, because Hercules was to be paid. So two more were added.
Hyperboreans were a legendary people living far north, beyond the north wind. Atlas here is a place or mountain, not only the Titan.
"Divers" means various or several; the dragon's voice took many different forms.
"To wit" is an archaic phrase meaning "that is to say" or "namely".
Nereus was a sea-god who could change shape and would tell the truth only if held fast until he yielded.
"Waxed" means grew; "so it was that" is archaic phrasing for "it happened that".
"Dearth" means a scarcity or famine.
"Haled" means dragged or hauled by force; an archaic form of "hauled".
Refers to a ritual in which Hercules' sacrifices at Lindos were accompanied by curses, explained as an echo of the cowherd's anger.
The goblet from the Sun is the golden cup Hercules used to cross the ocean, in connection with the cattle of Geryones.
The bond of olive refers to a wreath of olive Hercules wore as a substitute for Prometheus' chains; Chiron's exchange lets Prometheus go free.
The "sphere" is the celestial vault or heavens, which Atlas was condemned to hold up; elsewhere it is simply called the sky.
A "pad" is a cushion placed on the head to ease the weight of a load.
"Not lawful that they should be laid down anywhere": the apples were sacred to the gods and belonged only in the garden, so Athena returned them.
The sentence is elliptical: Hercules, a foreigner, got around the ban by being adopted by Pylius, an Athenian, so he could qualify.
The slaughter of the centaurs refers to Hercules' earlier fight with the centaurs, which left him ritually polluted and barred from the mysteries.
Taenarum, the southern tip of the Peloponnese (modern Cape Matapan), was believed to hold a cave entrance to the underworld.
"Wooed Persephone in wedlock" means Pirithous tried to win Persephone as his bride; Theseus joined this attempt and both were imprisoned.
Ascalaphus had testified that Persephone ate a pomegranate seed in Hades, so she had to stay; Demeter's anger had Hades's guard bury him under a stone.
Ghosts in Hades could speak only after drinking blood, so Hercules offers them blood to let them regain some awareness.
A cuirass is armor protecting the chest and back.
Demeter, goddess of grain and Persephone's mother, punished Ascalaphus for his testimony by changing him into an owl.

context_notes.text: Cycnus was a violent son of Ares, god of war, which explains why Ares backs him in the duel.
Zeus's thunderbolt ends the fight, showing the king of the gods intervening to protect his son Hercules.
Antaeus was a giant-like wrestler of Libya, whose strength came from contact with his mother Earth, as the next sentence explains.
Busiris was a legendary Egyptian king, a son of Poseidon, the sea god, known in myth for killing strangers.
Prometheus was punished by Zeus for giving fire to humans; an eagle ate his liver daily, and it grew back.
Prometheus was the Titan chained to the Caucasus for giving fire to humans; Hercules had freed him and so received his advice.
Cerberus was the hound guarding the entrance to Hades, the underworld; bringing him up was the last and hardest labour.
Eleusis, near Athens, was the home of the Eleusinian Mysteries, secret rites honoring Demeter and Persephone and promising a better fate after death.
Meleager was a hero of the Calydonian boar hunt; the Gorgon Medusa was a monster whose gaze petrified, here dead and a shade.
Pluto is the king of the dead (the Greek Hades). Cerberus was his three-headed watchdog.
Eurystheus was the king who set Hercules his twelve labors; fetching Cerberus was the last.

literary_notes.text: The golden apples, a wedding gift guarded by a monstrous dragon, symbolise divine treasure and the near-impossible nature of the task.
The shape-shifting god held until he gives answers recurs in Greek myth; Hercules' persistence shows endurance as his defining trait.
Antaeus's source of strength, contact with Earth, becomes his downfall once Hercules lifts him off the ground.
Busiris kills the seer who prescribed the sacrifice, first of all, so the prophet becomes the first victim of his own remedy.
The story explains a real cult custom by a mythic origin, giving the ritual curses a cause in Hercules' meal.
Atlas tries to trick Hercules and is himself tricked, so his scheme is turned against him, and the sentence shows Hercules' craft over strength.
The hybrid of dog heads, dragon tail and snake heads builds a monstrous picture that emphasizes the terror of the underworld.
The hero attacks a harmless phantom; his strength is useless against the dead, a moment of comic misjudgment.
The captives' gesture is compared to rising from death, stressing their hope and Hercules's great power.
Hercules's armor, lion skin and unrelenting grip show his endurance and stubborn strength in facing pain.
